question: In 2015, the International Agency for Research on Cancer, part of the World Health Organization, classified processed meats as Group 1 carcinogens due to strong evidence that the nitrites used in the curing process contribute to the formation of carcinogenic nitrosamines.

Ten years later, scientific evidence linking nitrite-cured meats to bowel, pancreatic and breast cancers has only strengthened, yet regulatory action across the EU remains limited. While lower nitrite limits recently came into force, they still leave consumers unnecessarily exposed to compounds with proven carcinogenic potential. 1.
Does the Commission intend to propose further measures to progressively restrict and phase out the use of nitrites in processed meats, with clear timelines and transitional support for producers?
Will it consider introducing mandatory, harmonised front-of-pack health warnings on nitrite-cured products to ensure consistent information and protection for consumers across Member States?

Will the Commission commit to funding comparative research and pilot projects to identify, validate and scale nitrite-free curing technologies, including support for SMEs to transition to safer alternatives?

Given the EU’s responsibility under Article 168 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union to ensure a high level of human health protection in all policies, further coherent EU action on nitrites would safeguard public health and support innovation in a more competitive, health-conscious food sector.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.1.2026) Based on epidemiological studies, the Monograph of the International Agency for Research on Cancer1 classifies processed meat as Group 1 carcinogen and recommends moderating its consumption. It also explores biological mechanisms that may play a role in colorectal cancer development2.
In its assessment3, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) concludes that nitrite additives4 are neither genotoxic nor carcinogenic and establishes an Acceptable Daily Intake value5.

The Commission does not intend to propose further measures on nitrite additives considering that the lower maximum levels6 applicable since October 2025 were adopted as a balanced outcome taking into account the risk of the formation of nitrosamines through the presence of nitrites in meat products and the protective effects of nitrites against pathogenic bacteria, while considering a broad variety of processed meat products available on the EU market.
However, the Commission is considering establishing limits and taking measures reducing the presence of nitrosamines in foods under the EU rules on contaminants.

The Commission does not consider front-of-pack health warnings on nitrite-cured products appropriate as according to EFSA, nitrite is not carcinogenic, and it is not possible to clearly discern the nitrosamines formed from the nitrite added as a food additive from those formed from the nitrite naturally present in the food or as result of contamination.

The Commission already supported research and innovation projects such as PHYTOME7, and NOCHEMFOOD8 to explore the replacement of nitrite additives. Other projects are conducted by Member States such as the project NitriFree9 which will end in 2026.
1 IARC Monographs, volume 114, Red Meat and Processed Meat. ISBN 978-92-832-0180-9. 2 The monograph particularly identifies the hazards such as (i) ‘haem iron’ a component of red meat, (ii)

‘nitrosamines’ substances that may be formed during the meat processing in the presence of nitrites and (iii) ‘heterocyclic aromatic amines’ and ‘polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons’, i.e. chemicals occurring at the hightemperature treatment. 3 EFSA Journal 2017;15(6):4786. 4 Potassium nitrite (E 249) and sodium nitrite (E 250).

5 EFSA defines ‘acceptable daily intake’ as an estimate of the amount of a substance in food or drinking water that can be consumed daily over a lifetime without presenting an appreciable risk to health: https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/glossary/acceptable-daily-intake.

6 Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/2108 of 6 October 2023 amending Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council and the Annex to Commission Regulation (EU) No 231/2012 as regards food additives nitrites (E 249-250) and nitrates (E 251-252) (OJ L, 2023/2108, 9.10.2023, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/2108/oj). 7 https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/315683/reporting.
8 Novel Vegetal-based Extracts Additives for CHEMical-Free FOOD: https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/23060. 9 NitriFree: https://www.ivlv.org/en/project/nitrifree/.
